title: The case for doing one thing at a time
text:
Many professionals are proud of their ability to multitask. They answer messages during meetings, write reports while listening to calls, and switch between a dozen tabs without a pause. Researchers who study attention, however, suggest that this habit is less efficient than it feels. Each time we change tasks, the brain needs a short period to refocus, and those small delays add up over a day.

Single-tasking is the opposite approach. You choose one task, close everything else, and work on it for a fixed period, often between thirty and ninety minutes. Messages can wait until the period ends. People who try this method often report that they make fewer mistakes and feel less exhausted by the afternoon.

The method is not perfect, of course. Some jobs, such as customer support, require constant availability, and a team cannot simply ignore urgent requests. Even so, most employees can protect a few quiet hours each week. A sensible first step is to tell colleagues when you will be unavailable and when you will reply, so that nobody feels ignored.

opts: The brain needs time to refocus after each change of task.
qs.why: The text says that each time we change tasks, the brain needs a short period to refocus.

opts: They are not suitable for anyone.

qs.why: They require constant availability, so long periods without answering are difficult.

qs.why: Small delays accumulate and become a significant amount of lost time.

title: My first week as a team leader
text:
Last Monday I became the leader of a small team of five people. I was excited, but I was also nervous. Until then, I had only worked on my own tasks, and now I was responsible for other people's work as well.

On the first day, I made a common mistake. I tried to solve every problem myself because I wanted to look strong. By Wednesday I was tired and behind schedule. Then an older colleague, Marta, gave me some simple advice. She said that a good leader does not do everything. A good leader asks questions, listens carefully, and trusts the team.

On Thursday I changed my approach. I asked each person what they needed from me, and I wrote down their answers. Two people wanted clearer goals, and one person wanted more time to finish a project. These requests were easy to fulfil, and the mood in the office improved immediately. I still have a lot to learn, but I feel more confident now. This week I am going to ask for feedback about my own work, because leaders need advice too.

title: Request to adjust the project timeline
text:
Dear Mr Alvarez,

Thank you for your message about the delivery date of the new reporting platform. I am writing to explain why we would like to discuss a revised timeline, and to propose a solution that I hope will suit both parties.

During last week's testing phase, our engineers identified a problem with the way the system handles large volumes of data. Although the issue is not critical, we believe that releasing the platform without resolving it would damage the experience of your staff. Fixing it properly will take approximately ten additional working days.

We appreciate that the original date was important to your department, so I would like to suggest a compromise. We could deliver the core features on the agreed date, and release the remaining functions two weeks later, once the improvements have been completed. In this way, your team could begin working with the platform without any further delay.

I would be grateful if we could arrange a short call tomorrow or on Thursday to talk this through. Please let me know which time is more convenient for you.

Kind regards,
Helena Duarte
Project Manager

title: The question nobody wanted to ask
text:
During my first month as an intern, I attended a long meeting about a new customer database. Everyone nodded while the director explained the plan, but I realised halfway through that I did not understand one important point. The plan seemed to depend on a tool that the company did not have.

I hesitated. I was the youngest person in the room, and I did not want to look foolish. However, the doubt kept growing, so eventually I raised my hand and asked, as politely as I could, which tool the team would use. There was a short silence. Then the director frowned, checked her notes, and admitted that she had forgotten to mention it.

To my surprise, several colleagues thanked me afterwards. One of them confessed that he had wondered about the same thing but had not dared to speak. The team then spent twenty minutes fixing the plan, and the project avoided a costly misunderstanding. Since that day I have remembered something useful. A question that feels embarrassing is often the question that other people are also thinking about. Asking it does not make you look weak. More often, it shows that you are paying attention.

opts: Asking a question can help everyone, even if it feels embarrassing.

title: Learning to live with my partner
text:
Three months ago, my partner Daniel and I moved into the same flat. We had dated for two years, and we thought that living together would be easy. In fact, it taught us a lot about each other.

The first surprise was the small daily habits. Daniel likes to wake up at six and go for a run, while I prefer to stay in bed until eight. He keeps the windows open all year, but I am always cold. At first, these differences annoyed us, and we argued about silly things such as who forgot to buy milk.

Then we decided to sit down and make a few simple rules. We share the housework equally, we cook dinner together on Fridays, and we each have one evening a week to spend alone or with friends. It sounds almost boring, but it works. Now I understand that love is not only about romantic dinners and holidays. It is also about being patient when the other person leaves a wet towel on the bed. If you are thinking about moving in with someone, my advice is to talk openly before the problems become big.

title: Why friendships get harder after thirty
text:
Making friends was easy at school. You saw the same people every day, you shared the same problems, and you had plenty of free time. In adult life, those conditions disappear. Jobs, children and long journeys leave little energy for new relationships, and old friends often move to other cities.

Sociologists point out that friendship usually grows from repeated contact in a relaxed setting. When that contact becomes rare, even strong friendships can weaken. This does not mean that people stop caring. It simply means that the habit of meeting has been lost, and rebuilding it takes some effort.

Fortunately, small actions can make a big difference. A short message to say that you were thinking of someone costs almost nothing, yet it often leads to a longer conversation. Regular activities, such as a weekly football match or a monthly dinner, give friendships a stable structure. They also remove the need to organise something new every time. Perhaps the most important step is to accept that friendships are not always equal. Sometimes one person has more time than the other. If both sides remain patient and generous, a friendship can survive long silences and return stronger than before.

qs.why: The text explains why adult friendships struggle and suggests ways to maintain them.

qs.why: Sociologists say friendship usually grows from repeated contact in a relaxed setting.

qs.why: Regular activities give a stable structure so nobody has to organise a new plan every time.

qs.why: A stable structure is one that stays steady and dependable.

title: The apology that came too late
text:
Ines had not spoken to her brother Paulo for six years. The argument that separated them had begun over their father's old house, but over time it had become something much larger, a collection of small resentments that neither of them could name. Each had waited for the other to call first, and the waiting had hardened into habit.

One evening, while she was tidying a drawer, Ines found a postcard that Paulo had sent her from a trip long ago. On the back he had written only a few words: "Wish you were here. The sea would make you laugh." She sat on the floor for a long time, holding the card, and she realised that she could no longer remember what had made her so angry.

She wrote a message, deleted it, and wrote another. In the end she sent three simple sentences. She said that she missed him, that she was sorry for her part in the quarrel, and that she hoped they could meet. His reply arrived the next morning. It was short, but it was warm. "I almost wrote to you last year," he said. "I am glad you did it first." Ines read it twice and smiled, aware that pride had cost them far too many years.

opts: Paulo was the only one at fault.
Pride kept two siblings apart until one of them chose to reach out.
qs.why: Both waited for the other to call first, until Ines chose to write.

qs.why: She found a postcard that Paulo had sent her from a trip long ago.

He did not want to meet her.

title: Why tipping customs differ around the world
text:
Visitors to a new country are often confused about tipping. In some places, leaving extra money at a restaurant is considered a basic duty. In others, it can seem strange or even slightly insulting. These differences are not random. They reflect history, wages and social expectations.

In countries where servers earn a low basic salary, tips make up a large part of their income, so customers feel responsible for adding to it. In countries where restaurants pay fair wages and include a service charge in the bill, an additional tip is usually seen as a small thank-you rather than an obligation. Some cultures also prefer to keep money and kindness separate, and they consider a friendly smile to be enough.

Travellers can avoid embarrassment with a little research. A guidebook or a quick conversation with a local resident will usually explain what is normal. When in doubt, it is wise to check the bill, because the service may already be included. Understanding these customs is not only about money. It is also a way of showing respect. When we follow local habits, we show that we are guests who care about the place we are visiting.

opts: Tipping customs depend on local wages and social expectations.
Servers earn more in some countries than in others because of the weather.

qs.why: The text explains that tipping habits reflect history, wages and expectations.

qs.why: The text says the service may already be included in the bill.

qs.q: What can we infer about countries with fair wages?

qs.why: There, a tip is seen as a small thank-you rather than an obligation.

qs.why: An obligation is a duty or something one is expected to do.

title: Why I went back to paper books
text:
For about ten years I read almost everything on a screen. It was convenient. I could carry hundreds of books in my bag, change the size of the letters, and buy a new title in seconds. Last year, however, I noticed that I was finishing fewer books than ever, and that I rarely remembered what I had read.

On a whim, I bought a paperback in a small second-hand shop. The pages were slightly yellow, and the cover had a coffee stain, but I enjoyed it more than anything I had read for months. Without notifications or tempting apps, I could simply sit with the story. I also found that I remembered where things happened in the book, for example that a certain scene was near the bottom of a left-hand page.

I have not abandoned my e-reader completely. It is still the best choice for travelling or for reading in the dark. Nevertheless, I now keep a pile of paper books next to my bed, and I treat them as a small ritual at the end of the day. Perhaps the lesson is not that paper is better than screens. It is that the way we read shapes how deeply we read.

title: Dinner at the Okafors'
text:
When I moved to a new city for work, my neighbour Mrs Okafor invited me to dinner on my second evening. I accepted at once, although I felt a little shy. I had never visited a Nigerian family, and I was afraid of doing something wrong.

The table was full of dishes I could not name, and the smell of pepper and spices filled the room. Mrs Okafor's husband explained that it was polite to serve the oldest guest first, so my plate arrived before anyone else's, which made me blush. When I tried to refuse a second helping, the whole family laughed and told me that in their home a guest who stopped eating after one plate was probably unhappy.

Between courses, they asked about my family, my work and my favourite music. I discovered that their eldest daughter was a doctor and that their son played in a jazz band. By the end of the evening I had forgotten my nervousness completely. Walking back to my flat, I realised that hospitality does not need a common language or a shared background. It needs only an open door and a willingness to share what you have. I have never felt so welcome in a city I barely knew.

title: Is public Wi-Fi safe?
text:
Many cafes, airports and hotels offer free Wi-Fi, and most of us connect without thinking. It is certainly convenient, but public networks can also be risky. Because many strangers use the same connection, a dishonest person may be able to see some of the information that you send.

The danger is not the same for every activity. Reading the news or watching a video is usually not a problem. Entering a password, checking your bank account or filling in a form with personal details is different, because that information could be useful to a criminal.

Fortunately, a few simple habits can reduce the risk. First, check the name of the network with a member of staff, because criminals sometimes create a fake network with a similar name. Second, use websites that start with https, which means that the connection is protected. Third, consider using a VPN, a service that hides your activity from other people on the network. If you must do something important and you are not sure about the network, the safest option is to use your mobile data instead. It may use a little of your allowance, but it can save you a lot of trouble.

opts: Public Wi-Fi is convenient but needs some precautions.
Mobile data is cheaper than Wi-Fi.
qs.why: The text explains the risks and then gives simple habits to reduce them.

qs.why: Entering passwords or personal details can give useful information to criminals.

A criminal may create a fake network with a similar name.
qs.why: Fake networks with similar names exist, so staff can confirm the real one.

qs.why: To reduce the risk is to make it smaller.

title: Action required: mandatory security update
text:
Subject: Action required by Friday: mandatory security update

Dear colleagues,

As part of our ongoing effort to protect company and customer data, the IT department will install an important security update on all laptops this week. The update closes several weaknesses that attackers could otherwise use to gain access to our systems.

To make the process as smooth as possible, please follow these steps. First, save your work and close all your applications before you leave the office on Thursday. Second, leave your laptop connected to the power supply and to the office network overnight, so that the update can install without interruption. Finally, restart the computer when you arrive on Friday morning and check that the new version number appears on the login screen.

Please note that we will never ask for your password by email or by telephone. If you receive a message that seems to come from us and requests your login details, do not reply. Forward it to the security team instead.

If your laptop has not been updated by Friday at noon, or if you notice any problems afterwards, contact the service desk through the internal portal. A technician will help you as soon as possible.

Thank you for your cooperation.

Best regards,
The IT Security Team

To explain how to install a security update on laptops.
To ask employees for their passwords.
qs.why: The email explains the update and the steps employees should follow.

qs.why: The first step is to save work and close applications before leaving on Thursday.

title: Machine translation and the human translator
text:
Only a few years ago, automatic translation often produced sentences that were awkward or even funny. Today the results are much better. Free tools can translate an email, a menu or a webpage in a moment, and the output is usually clear enough to understand. This progress has led many people to ask whether professional translators will still be needed.

The answer seems to be yes, although their work is changing. Machines handle simple, repetitive text very well, but they struggle with humour, cultural references and subtle differences in tone. A legal contract or a novel requires someone who understands not only the words, but also the situation behind them. A small mistake in such a document can have serious consequences.

Many translators now use the software as an assistant. The machine produces a first version, and the human reviews it, corrects errors and improves the style. This can save time, and it allows translators to concentrate on the parts that need judgement. For language learners, these tools are useful but should be used carefully. They can help you check a word quickly. However, if you rely on them for every sentence, you will have fewer opportunities to practise thinking in the new language.

qs.why: The text mentions humour, cultural references and subtle differences in tone.

title: What happened when my class used an AI tutor
text:
This term, I tried an experiment with my class of sixteen-year-olds. Each student could ask an AI assistant for help with their history essays, as long as they told me exactly how they had used it. I expected a disaster, but the results were more interesting than I had imagined.

Some students used the tool to copy whole paragraphs, and their essays sounded strangely similar. I quickly noticed this, because the writing did not match the way they spoke in class. Others, however, used the assistant as a patient partner. They asked it to explain difficult words, suggest questions to research, or point out where an argument was unclear. Their essays improved, and they seemed more confident when we discussed them.

The difference was not the technology but the habit of the student. Those who treated the tool as a shortcut learned little. Those who treated it as a coach learned a great deal. Based on this, I have changed my rules. Students must now write a first draft without any help, and only then can they ask the assistant for feedback. I still have concerns, but I no longer believe that banning the tool is the best answer. Teaching students to use it wisely seems more realistic.

qs.why: The text says the writing did not match the way they spoke in class.

opts: The teacher wants students to think for themselves first.

title: Using an AI assistant to write my emails
text:
I work in a small company, and I write about thirty emails every day. Some of them are easy, but others take me a long time, especially when I have to be polite and clear in English. A few weeks ago, a colleague suggested that I try an AI assistant, so I decided to test it.

The first result was impressive. I gave the assistant a few notes about a late delivery, and it wrote a friendly and professional message in seconds. However, when I read the email carefully, I noticed a problem. The assistant had promised a new delivery date that I had never mentioned. If I had sent it without checking, my customer would have expected something that I could not provide.

Since then, I use the assistant in a different way. I write the main points myself, ask it to improve the style, and always read the final text before I press send. This method saves me about an hour a day, and my emails sound more natural. My conclusion is simple. The tool is a very good helper, but it is not responsible for what I send. I am, so I must always check the details.
